title: Can a flag count tell these tickets apart?

beats.say: A customer reports a page stuck loading. Punch the slow-page flag on the blue ticket. Feed it through a counter that saves one number. It reads one.
The pink ticket asks for a rollback. Its hole sits in the other column. What number will the same counter save?
One again. Put the two readings side by side. One ticket needs the performance team and the other needs release repair. What measurement would preserve that difference?

title: Give the tickets two coordinates

beats.say: Read each ticket from left to right. The first flag records slow pages. The second records a request to roll back. A third customer reported both. Watch each row become a point. The point keeps the order of the features. Keep that order when the next ticket enters the reader.

Suppose we just want the rollback ticket. Select its row by its ticket ID and take both entries. An embedding table works the same way. A token ID selects one learned vector. A different operation, matrix multiplication, reads matching positions across a row and a column to compute a new score.

title: Build a point from two directions

beats.say: Blue adds an equal amount to both features. Pink takes from slow pages and adds to rollback. Shrink both arrows to unit length so we can compare a step in either direction. They meet at a right angle. A basis is a set of independent directions whose combinations reach every point in the space. Unit lengths and right angles make this basis orthonormal.

For this example, count mentions. Three mentions of slow pages and one of rollback give the row three, one. The dot product with each unit arrow tells us how far to travel along it. Build the common contribution, then add the contrast at its tip.
If you could save only the common part, where would the ticket land?

Let the pink part fall away. The ticket lands at two and two. The missing part meets the blue line at a right angle. Sliding to either side would take us farther from the original ticket. The nearest point on that line is its orthogonal projection.

title: Measure what one direction produces

beats.say: Go back to the three rows of yes-or-no flags. Which direction would rebuild that table most faithfully? Divide the sum of the flags by the square root of two, so the common ruler has unit length. Each ticket contributes one dot product. Multiply each flag by its matching ruler entry, then add. Read the three scores from top to bottom.
Square the three scores and add. Each single-issue row contributes a half. The joint ticket alone supplies two of the three units of squared length.

title: Apply the contrast direction

beats.say: Try contrast. The slow-only ticket scores below zero. The rollback-only ticket scores just as far above zero. The joint ticket contains one of each. Where should its mark go?

Its two contributions cancel. There is the zero mark. Only the single-issue tickets add anything to the squared length. The squared total is one. Taking square roots gives output lengths of root three and one. These lengths are the singular values for the common and contrast directions.

title: Let the columns reveal their directions

beats.say: Where did those diagonals come from? Look down the original slow and rollback columns. Each column pair contributes one entry. Take the slow column twice. Count the links between ones. Two tickets have the slow flag. Write two at the upper left. Now compare slow with rollback. Only the joint ticket has both. Write one at the upper right. Reverse the two columns. How many links do you see?

One link, from the same joint ticket. Write one at the lower left. Finally compare rollback with itself. Count the rollback-only ticket and the joint ticket. That makes two. The finished table of column dot products is the Gram matrix, A transpose A.

title: What does the Gram matrix do to each arrow?

beats.say: Apply that Gram matrix to our two unit arrows. Common stretches along its own line. Contrast stays where it is. A nonzero vector that the matrix scales along its own line is an eigenvector. Its scale factor is its eigenvalue.
For a Gram matrix and a unit eigenvector, that factor equals the squared length of the original table's output. Square roots recover the singular strengths.

title: SVD, first move: change coordinates

beats.say: We can now describe what the table does to any input. The three moves are called singular value decomposition, or SVD. Start with the slow-page input, one, zero. Rotate the tracing into common and contrast coordinates. V transpose takes the dot product with each of those unit directions. Look where the green tip lands. Its common coordinate is positive and its contrast coordinate is negative.

title: Second move: stretch the coordinates

beats.say: Now stretch the common coordinate by its singular strength, square root of three. Leave contrast unchanged. Sigma turns the circle into an ellipse. The grid changes shape, and the same green input changes with it.

title: Third move: build the three-ticket output

beats.say: Carry the two stretched coordinates over from the ellipse. Each one scales a unit column of U. We got those columns by dividing each track of ticket scores by its singular strength. Read down a column in ticket order. Start with common. Multiply its positive coordinate by the common column. For the middle ticket the two factors give one half. Put that track on the reader. Now take contrast. Its coordinate is negative. The middle entry of its unit column is positive. Their product is minus one half. Add the contrast track. The middle channel falls back to zero. The final scores pick out exactly the tickets with the slow-page flag.

title: Two sign flips leave the answer fixed

beats.say: Reverse the common input arrow and its matching output arrow. The coordinate changes sign when we read it with the reversed input arrow. Multiplying by the reversed output arrow cancels that sign. Watch the output readings as the pair flips. Two correct SVD implementations can print different signs. Reconstruct the matrix to compare them.

title: Spend the one-number budget

beats.say: Go back to the router. Keep the common score for each ticket and shrink contrast to zero. The slow ticket slides in from one side. The rollback ticket comes from the other. Each single saves one over the square root of two. The joint ticket saves the square root of two. Hand the saved scores to a routing rule. Can it still send the two single-issue tickets to different teams?

The rule gets the same number twice. To see what the loss cost, multiply a saved score by the shared common direction. For a single-issue ticket that gives a half in each flag position. Read off the rebuilt rows. Four entries miss by a half. Square those misses, add them and take the square root. The Frobenius reconstruction error is one.
That is the smallest error possible at rank one. The router still needs to distinguish the first two tickets.

title: Who gets the second search result?

beats.say: Search for slow pages. Two tickets match that description. The slow ticket comes first and the ticket with both issues comes second. Cosine divides the dot product by both vector lengths. The result is the cosine of the angle between two nonzero vectors. Remove contrast from the tickets and the query.
All three now point the same way. With ties broken in ticket order, which two will search return?

Take the first two in ticket order. Rollback gets the slot the joint ticket used to have. We found one of the two relevant tickets. Recall at two has fallen from one to one half. On held-out searches, use the same projection for documents and queries. Compare recall with your release threshold.

You can score a whole batch this way. Return to the full feature rows and normalize each vector to unit length. Put a slow query and a rollback query in separate rows. Multiply by the transposed ticket table. Each cell compares one query with one ticket. With two queries and three tickets, that's six comparisons. Comparing every row of a table with every row of the same table takes a square grid.

title: Move the origin to the average ticket

beats.say: Read these as mention counts. Each flagged issue occurs once in its ticket. Slow pages come up twice. So does rollback. That's two thirds of a mention per ticket in each column. The gold cross marks that average. Subtract it from every row and watch the cross move to the origin.
The triangle keeps its shape. Each point now shows how a ticket differs from the average. This is centering in principal component analysis, or PCA.

title: Which direction varies most around the average?

beats.say: Project the centered points onto common. The two single-issue tickets land on exactly the same mark. Square the distances from zero and add them. Now turn the measuring stick toward contrast and repeat. The single-issue marks separate. Could a direction between these two give us even more spread?

Look at the two scores for each ticket. Start with slow pages. Both scores are negative, so their product is positive, one sixth. Next take rollback. Its common score is still negative but its contrast score is positive. Their product is minus one sixth. Now take the joint ticket. Its contrast score is zero, so its product is zero. Add the three products. The sum is zero, so the centered Gram matrix has zero off the diagonal in this basis.

Both rulers are eigenvectors. Contrast has three times the squared spread of common. A unit ruler between them takes a weighted average of those two spreads, with weights that sum to one. It cannot exceed the larger one. That's why SVD on this centered table picks contrast as its first principal direction.

title: A new ticket uses the fitted coordinate system

beats.say: Keep counting mentions, just as we did for training. Both dots start at their raw coordinates. The slow-only ticket had one slow mention and no rollback. A new ticket mentions slow pages twice and rollback once. Subtract the saved training mean from both rows. The two dots move together.
Each count went up by one compared with the slow-only ticket. Where will its mark land on the fitted ruler?
Now read the new ticket along the pink direction. The two marks meet. Both scores are minus one over the square root of two. Adding one mention of each issue leaves the difference unchanged.

To project future rows, use the training units and mean, then take a dot product with each saved row of V transpose. For example, to keep sixty-four features, place the first sixty-four right singular directions in columns and multiply your centered rows by that matrix. U describes the training tickets. Rescaling a feature before fitting can change which direction wins.

title: Centering changes the storage story, too

beats.say: Each row of this word-count table has just one stored entry. Look at the empty cells. Subtract a nonzero column mean and those empty cells fill. Here six stored values become thirty-six. Explicit centering can overwhelm memory. Sparse-aware PCA can subtract the mean's contribution during multiplication. Uncentered truncated SVD works directly with sparse input and measures energy around zero. Choose the origin that answers your question.

title: Can two weights fit three severity scores?

beats.say: Try one point for slow pages and two for rollback. The gold rings show observed severity. Each weight controls one column of three contributions. Our weights hit the first two rings exactly. What severity will they predict for the ticket with both flags?

One plus two gives three. Look at the gap to the ring. The observed severity is two. Changing the two weights moves our three readings in a plane. Move the prediction to the closest point in that plane.
Both weights come down by a third, to two thirds and five thirds. Now each prediction misses by just a third. Squaring those three misses and adding gives one third. This is the least-squares fit.

The pink residual runs from the fitted prediction to the target. Follow the slow column. Increasing its weight helps the first ticket but hurts the joint ticket by just as much at first. The rollback column makes the same trade. The residual is perpendicular to both columns.
Any further move in the plane increases squared error.

title: Two columns can carry one direction

beats.say: Make the second feature a copy of the first. Read the two columns like tracks on a recording. Raising either gain now changes exactly the same samples. Sweep the first gain and then the second. Both move the prediction along the same line. The table still has two columns. Only one singular value is nonzero. Counting those surviving directions gives the rank. Here the copy is exact. With measured data, numerical rank also depends on the threshold you choose for a small singular value.

title: Fit the same target after the plane collapses

beats.say: Fit the same severity target with the duplicate columns. The middle prediction is stuck at zero. The first and third tickets now share one prediction, the sum of the two weights. Move to the closest point.
Halfway between their targets of one and two gives the best fit for both. What does that tell us about the individual weights?

title: Different weights, identical predictions

beats.say: Keep the sum at one and a half. Increase one gain and decrease the other equally. Watch the green trace. The gains trade off while the pulse height stays fixed at every sample. This change lies in the nullspace. Multiplying the change in weights by the matrix gives zero. How many equally good gain pairs could the recording explain?

There is a whole line of equally good fits. A minimum-norm least-squares solver chooses the pair nearest the origin. Return both gains to three quarters. Every prediction still agrees. The recording determines their sum. The individual gains remain ambiguous.

Here's an experiment that can distinguish the gains. Set the gains to a quarter and one and a quarter. Suppose we delay the second input by one sample. Which channel would you hear first, and which crest would be taller?

The first channel would sound first, and the second crest would be taller. Open the delay. Read the quarter-height crest from A and the one-and-a-quarter crest from B. Each crest isolates one input, so its height gives that input's gain directly.

title: What happens when we reverse this map?

beats.say: Keep the horizontal axis and shrink the other a hundredfold. A circle becomes a thin ellipse. Imagine recovering the circle from that measurement. You would have to stretch the short axis back. For this invertible map, the strongest stretch divided by the weakest gives its two-norm condition number. An exactly zero singular value would make inversion impossible.

title: A small output wobble becomes a large input error

beats.say: Start with the clean reading on the enlarged ruler. Add a small output disturbance along the weak direction. Now reverse the map. The original coordinate was two tenths. The estimate lands at three tenths. Dividing by the small stretch turned a thousandth of measurement noise into a tenth of input error.

title: What survives rounding before a solve?

beats.say: Take two almost identical measurements. Send the same noisy measurements down both routes. The second reading picked up one extra thousandth. The direct least-squares path keeps the original table. Subtract the first row from the second. Only four hundredths of the second weight survive. That is enough to fit both readings, including their noise.

The other route forms the Gram matrix from the two columns. For the right-hand side, take the dot product of each original column with the observed readings. The first column counts both readings once. The second gives the second reading a little more weight. Carry those two sums into the equations.

Multiply the first equation by one point zero two and subtract it from the second. The first weight drops out. The second weight is a ratio of two tiny leftovers. Suppose we store each equation to only three decimal places. Which fit will change?

Introduce the storage rounding. The original table and the readings already fit in three decimal places. Round the normal equations before subtracting. The coefficient left after elimination grows from eight ten-thousandths to twelve ten-thousandths. The right-hand remainder shrinks from point zero zero one six two to point zero zero one three eight. Dividing the second by the first now gives a much smaller second weight.

Look where the two weights went. One rose as the other fell, even while their predictions stay close to the measurements. For independent columns, forming the Gram matrix squares the two-norm condition number. More stored digits help with this rounding.
A direct QR or SVD fit avoids that extra step. The original measurement noise still affects the direct fit.

title: Square the strengths before choosing a cutoff

beats.say: Suppose another table has singular values six, three and one. Each square shows how much that direction contributes to reconstruction. Count their areas. Thirty-six plus nine plus one gives forty-six. Predict the smallest retained rank that reaches ninety-five percent.

The first strength retains thirty-six over forty-six, about seventy-eight percent. The first two retain forty-five over forty-six, about ninety-eight percent. So two is the smallest rank that passes. For the Frobenius error, add the discarded squares and take the square root. That last square has area one.
On centered data the retained fraction measures variation around the mean. On the original table it measures energy around zero.

The last square barely moves the fraction. Think of the two tickets the router mixed up. A small discarded direction can still decide which team gets called. Before accepting a smaller search index, check the projected tickets and queries against the relevance judgments.

title: Two thin factors restrict the update’s directions

beats.say: Consider a model update that passes through a single number. Turn the input arrow all the way around. The first factor reads one coordinate. The second multiplies a fixed output direction by that number. The output travels back and forth along one line. Low-rank adaptation, or LoRA, learns the two thin factors of an update directly.
The width between them limits how many independent output directions it can use. The input and output widths also bound its rank.

Now let eight numbers pass between the factors. The full layer has four thousand ninety-six inputs and just as many outputs. Each factor has eight weights for each of those four thousand ninety-six positions. Counting both factors gives sixty-five thousand five hundred thirty-six in total.
The full square has over sixteen million weights. Those counts cover the update weights for one layer.

Pick one of those trainable weights. If we train it with Adam, it also needs two moment estimates. One tracks its gradient and the other tracks its squared gradient. Both are moving averages that give recent steps more weight.
Each weight in the two factors gets its own pair. Choose the rank by measuring how well the adapted model does its job.

title: Which measurement belongs in the field?

beats.say: Try two new tickets. One mentions slow pages four times. The other asks for a rollback four times. The yellow ruler measures their common score. You have one field to save. How would you set the ruler so the router can tell these tickets apart?
Turn it through a right angle. Watch the two marks on the score scale. They started together. Now contrast gives opposite signs, enough to separate these two issue types.
Leave the ruler there. A counter needs the total number of mentions in each ticket. Try zero, zero and four, four. Read the two stored scores. Could the counter recover both totals?

Both have contrast coordinate zero. Turn back to the common direction. Now the marks separate. Multiply each common score by the square root of two to recover the totals zero and eight. This is true for any pair of counts, because common adds the two entries before dividing by the square root of two.

title: Which tickets can one score route?

beats.say: Back at the support desk, pull up the original flags. They are yes or no, and every ticket has at least one. Restore contrast by turning the measuring direction. Save that score and file the notes. The router can read one number per ticket. If it reads zero, who should take the call?

Now apply the routing rule. Negative goes to performance. Positive goes to release repair. Zero goes to both teams. Zero means the two flags agree. Since every ticket here has a flag, both must be set.

Now the desk starts taking billing questions. A customer asks for an invoice. Neither flag is set. Compare its contrast score with the joint ticket's score. Could the router send one to billing and the other to both teams?
Both read zero. Give the slow flag one point and the rollback flag two points. Add the points for each ticket. Billing gets zero, and both teams get three.

Four codes take two bits, just like the original flags. Read the left bit for rollback and the right bit for slow pages. With both bits set, both teams get the ticket. Before choosing a smaller representation, name two cases that need different actions. Pass them through the encoder and check that the difference survives.
